name: Oklahoma Voice
title: New Oklahoma laws take effect on Sunday
text:
An adult Carolina mantis is pictured on a plant. Oklahoma lawmakers have made the Carolina mantis the state predator insect. (Photo by Grandbrothers/Getty Images)OKLAHOMA CITY – More than 200 new laws take effect Sunday following a legislative session that ended in May.
Oklahoma’s newest laws run the gamut from ones designed to protect children to requiring GPS monitoring for some domestic violence defendants to new state symbols.
Here’s a few of them: 
Ban on all childhood marriage 
Senate Bill 504 sets the marital age at 18.
The measure repeals all exceptions for minors getting married, including allowing matrimony with parental permission or with a court’s permission. Existing law allowed children 16 or under to be married with a judge’s permission.
The measure passed the state House by a single vote.
“It is one more thing we can do to protect children from predators,” said Sen. Warren Hamilton, R-McCurtain.
Sen. Warren Hamilton, R-McCurtain, listens to the governor’s State of the State Address on Feb. 3, 2025, in the House chamber of the state Capitol. (Photo by Kyle Phillips/For Oklahoma Voice)
He said the measure will help preserve the dignity of marriage.
“Marriage is the biggest decision a lot of people will make,” Hamilton said.
Oklahoma becomes the 17th state to ban child marriage. 
Visitation changes
Senate Bill 2170 adds sexual abuse to the list of reasons why supervised visitation shall be required.
Under the new law, anyone who has had
substantiated findings by the Department of Human Services of  of sexualabuse of a child will be required to have a third party present when having visitation with a child.
New state symbols
Some new laws add to the state’s growing list of symbols.
Senate Bill 2159 designates wheat as the state crop.
Meanwhile, Senate Bill 2065, dubbed the “Lucile Morehouse Pollinator Act,” designates the European honeybee as the agricultural pollinator, the American bumblebee the native insect, the Carolina mantis as the predator insect, and the rainbow scarab, a dung beetle, as the soil conservation insect.
Morehouse and her mother started the Lucile’s Pollinator Project after learning that pollinators were in decline. The project provides free seeds.
Weakening the governor’s appointment powers 
Senate Bill 1327 restores the Oklahoma Tourism and Recreation Commission’s power to appoint the head of the Oklahoma Department of Tourism and Recreation.
It removes the governor’s power to make the appointment.
The action comes after the agency was embroiled in a scandal in which a restaurant vendor was convicted of defrauding the state of millions by submitting inflated invoices.
The agency head will serve at the pleasure of the commission instead of the governor, according to the measure.
Tracking domestic violence offenders
Senate Bill 1325 requires certain defendants charged with domestic violence offenses, who are released on bond, to wear a global positioning device that can be tracked by the victim.
Sen. Bill Coleman, R-Ponca City, is the author. Coleman said he talked to a number of judges who thought the measure could save lives.
Sen. Bill Coleman, R-Ponca City, sits at his desk on the Senate floor on May 21, 2025 ahead of the swearing in ceremony for a newly elected senator. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)
If a victim were able to have advance warning that the defendant was approaching their home or business, it would allow the victim to get to a safe location, Coleman said.
Marijuana packaging changes
House Bill 4454 prohibits edible marijuana packaging from being attractive to people under 18. It prohibits the use of cartoons, toys, animals and food to sell the product. It also bars the product from being shaped like commercially available candy.
Jed Green, director for Oklahomans for Responsible Cannabis Action, said laws like the one created by HB 4454 can be a little subjective.
“I would urge folks in the industry to err on the side of caution,” Green said. 
Rep. Carl Newton, R-Cherokee, said the measure also requires the products to list the content of Tetrahydrocannabinol, or THC, the psychoactive element of marijuana, to help prevent over medication.
Adoptions and gender-affirming care
House Bill 3586 prohibits the denial of adoption based on the parents’ refusal to enable the child to accessgender-affirming care.
Raising the child consistent with the child’s biological sex does not constitute abuse, according to the measure.
A new bridge
House Bill 2123 allows the Oklahoma Turnpike Authority to build a new bridge crossing the Arkansas River in the Bixby area.
Rep. Mark Tedford, R-Tulsa, said the measure empowers the agency to start surveying and evaluating locations for their portion of the project.
Rep. Mark Tedford, R-Tulsa, front, and Sen. Adam Pugh, R-Edmond, back, wait in line for candidate filing on April 1, 2026, at the state Capitol in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
Additional roads would need to be built by local entities, he said.
“It is going to be a team effort to get the proper funding and get the whole project done,” Tedford said.
‘True Grit Trail’
House Bill 1411 establishes the True Grit Trail in southeast Oklahoma.
“True Grit” is a novel written by Arkansas-born author Charles Portis that depicts 14-year-old Mattie Ross’ efforts to avenge her father’s murder. It was made into a 1969 movie featuring the late John Wayne who plays U.S. Marshall Reuben J. “Rooster” Cogburn.
Much of the story was set in Oklahoma, said Rep. Jim Grego, R-Wilburton, in a statement.
“This new trail will give us a way to show off the places made popular in the story and  hopefully will draw new visitors to this area of the state,” Grego said. “This could positively impact our local hotels, restaurants and other businesses.”
Towns and places of interest along the trail include: Sallisaw, Spiro, Bokoshe, McCurtain, Kinta, Quinton, Krebs, McAlester, Hartshorne, Wilburton, Red Oak, Bengal, Talihina, Robbers Cave State Park and the Talimena National Scenic Byway.

name: California
title: Cómo la Proposición 45 podría alterar las luchas en California contra los centros de datos
text:
This article is also available in English. Read it here.
Los votantes de California que estén considerando la Proposición 45 decidirán el destino de una medida de infraestructura de gran alcance que, según advierten sus opositores, podría dejar prácticamente sin efecto las nuevas leyes estatales sobre centros de datos.
 Eso facilitaría enormemente que los promotores inmobiliarios impongan instalaciones no deseadas en las comunidades locales, lo que podría socavar una creciente ola de prohibiciones, moratorias y resoluciones contra los centros de datos a nivel municipal y de condado.
 Los defensores de los centros de datos insisten en que la medida electoral no les reportará ningún beneficio, incluso cuando algunos beneficiarios de los centros de datos están invirtiendo grandes sumas de dinero para respaldar la Proposición 45.
 Los partidarios de la Proposición 45 la han presentado como una herramienta para acelerar proyectos de infraestructura crítica , como viviendas y escuelas, y la medida no menciona directamente los centros de datos entre los tipos de proyectos que considera críticos. Sin embargo, algunos expertos legales y defensores del medio ambiente afirman que el lenguaje técnico de la proposición crea una laguna legal. Al agilizar las evaluaciones ambientales bajo la Ley de Calidad Ambiental de California para amplias categorías de proyectos —incluidas las instalaciones de internet de banda ancha y cualquier infraestructura adicional necesaria para su funcionamiento—, la medida podría permitir discretamente que los centros de datos eludan las recientes salvaguardias estatales y el escrutinio local.
 Julia Stein, experta en derecho y subdirectora del Instituto Emmett sobre Cambio Climático y Medio Ambiente de la Facultad de Derecho de UCLA, advierte que la medida actúa como un “instrumento de fuerza bruta en lo que respecta a la racionalización” debido a la amplitud de su ámbito de aplicación secundario.
 “Lo que hace la Proposición 45 es designar toda una categoría de proyectos que estarían sujetos a una simplificación, y también establece que los proyectos auxiliares a esos proyectos —es decir, algo que podría ser necesario hacer durante el desarrollo del proyecto que está exento— quedarían incluidos en esa misma simplificación”, dijo Stein.
 Los proyectos de telecomunicaciones se simplifican explícitamente según la propuesta, “y hay argumentos para considerar que el desarrollo de centros de datos podría ser necesario para proyectos de ese tipo”, añadió Stein.
 Otros proyectos, como el tren de alta velocidad, quedan explícitamente excluidos de la simplificación de trámites según la propuesta, pero los centros de datos tampoco figuran en esa lista. Stein y otros tres expertos en derecho ambiental declararon a CalMatters que esto abre la puerta a posibles impugnaciones legales.
 “El hecho de que hayan excluido algunos proyectos, pero no hayan excluido expresamente los centros de datos, probablemente un tribunal lo interpretaría no como un descuido involuntario, sino más bien como una intención de incluir los centros de datos en la iniciativa”, dijo Matt McKerley, abogado de Shute, Mihaly y Weinberger.
 Además, los opositores argumentan que la redacción de la propuesta, que incluye una cláusula que establece que prevalecería sobre otras leyes relacionadas, anularía medidas como el Proyecto de Ley 887 del Senado , aprobado recientemente, que dificultó la tramitación acelerada de la revisión ambiental para los centros de datos.
 Los representantes del sector afirman que estas objeciones a la Proposición 45 son infundadas. La Coalición de Centros de Datos, un grupo industrial que apoya la Proposición 45, insiste en que sus instalaciones quedan fuera del alcance de la iniciativa, que se centra principalmente en el desarrollo de viviendas y otras infraestructuras como carreteras y puentes.
 “La Coalición de Centros de Datos ha revisado la Proposición 45 y ha llegado a la conclusión de que los centros de datos no cumplen los requisitos para la simplificación que contempla la Proposición 45, ni son una entidad cubierta por ninguna parte de la medida”, dijo Khara Boender, Directora de Asuntos Gubernamentales para la Región Oeste de la coalición.
 Los representantes del sector también hacen referencia a un reciente dictamen jurídico de la Oficina de Asesoría Legislativa de California, que presta servicios legales a los miembros de la Legislatura. El dictámenes argumenta que las definiciones legales de la Proposición 45 no se aplican a los centros de datos.
 Amelia Matier, de la campaña “Sí a la Proposición 45”, se hizo eco de esa opinión, afirmando: “Los centros de datos no están incluidos en la Proposición 45”. Añadió: “Los defensores del inasequible statu quo de California están desesperados por distraer a los votantes con mentiras porque no pueden justificar las costosas demoras y la burocracia que elevan los precios para las familias trabajadoras “ .
 Entre los opositores a la medida se encuentran la Federación Laboral de California, el Centro Occidental de Derecho y Pobreza, y varios grupos de defensa del medio ambiente que han gastado más de 31 millones de dólares para oponerse a la medida.
A pesar de sostener que los centros de datos quedan fuera del alcance de la propuesta, los intereses tecnológicos y de servicios públicos que se benefician del auge informático de California están impulsando su aprobación con un enorme apoyo financiero . Los defensores han invertido más de 40 millones de dólares en la campaña a favor de la Proposición 45, incluyendo 3.05 millones de dólares del gigante de servicios públicos PG&E y 500,000 dólares del desarrollador de almacenes y centros de datos Prologis; una inyección de capital que, según los opositores, revela quién espera realmente beneficiarse si la medida se aprueba.
 El debate sobre el impacto de la Proposición 45 en los centros de datos surge en un momento crucial del auge de la infraestructura de IA en California. El gobernador Gavin Newsom firmó recientemente siete leyes históricas sobre centros de datos destinadas a obligar a los operadores a revelar su consumo de agua, financiar sus propias mejoras de la red eléctrica y someterse a una evaluación ambiental.
 Sin embargo, las comunidades locales no esperan a que entren en vigor las regulaciones estatales. Ante el creciente temor a las subidas de tarifas, la sobrecarga de la red eléctrica y el agotamiento del agua, ha surgido una fuerte oposición ciudadana en toda California. Al menos 26 ciudades y condados han propuesto o aprobado moratorias, prohibiciones o límites estrictos destinados a frenar la construcción de centros de datos en sus comunidades.
 Nina Robertson, abogada adjunta de la oficina regional de Earthjustice en California, afirmó que la ambigüedad del texto de la papeleta electoral desencadenaría de inmediato batallas legales sobre la autoridad local para otorgar permisos.
 “¿Y quién va a asumir el coste de ese litigio?”, preguntó Robertson. “Serán los gobiernos locales”.

name: VTDigger
title: Tax the rich to spare the rest of us
text:
Dear Editor,
There is one single, fundamental issue underlying the election next week, and many people speak a partial truth about it: Our taxes are too high. Agreed; for most Vermonters, they are.  
But some people’s taxes are too low. The wealthiest among us have not paid their fair share to properly support our society in generations, if ever. Not in Vermont, and not in the U.S.  
According to data from the Vermont Department of Taxes, the number of Vermont income tax filers earning more than $300,000 in 2015 was 3,519, just under 1% of all taxpayers. By 2024, this fortunate group had grown to 9,788, constituting just over 2.5% of taxpayers. In 2015, they collectively paid 6.93% of their income to the state, and in 2024 they paid 6.73%. During that time, their collective income nearly tripled. 
By my calculation, if this wealthiest cohort paid just 2% more, that would be about half what it would take to render taxes on anyone earning under $100,000 unnecessary. If they paid 6.2% more, no one making under $150,000 would need to pay taxes. That’s about 90% of us.
Is anyone proposing to tax the rich so hard they worry about affording heat this winter? Or keeping their cars running? Or even taxing them enough that they might worry about affording a vacation? No, of course not. 
Why, then, is it fair to tax any Vermonters to the point that any of us must have such fears?

READ MORE

Let’s compromise and consider taxing the rich just enough so their increased payments let us lower everyone else’s taxes and relieve everyone of such fears. In the process, we would fund our schools, roads and social services to a level where all Vermonters can start to feel that we live in a healthy state where everyone shares in the work.
We should each pay, within our means, toward the well-being of Vermont and its people. There is obviously a deep unfairness in our system when hardworking people are taxed so hard that it hurts, while wealthy people are not. 
If you want change, don’t get distracted by the implementation details. We will only get the chance for change if we elect people willing to effect change. The wealthy and comfortable buy our land and our houses; they vacation here and, yes, many make tax-deductible contributions to the nonprofits trying to provide a safety net. The wealthy own the TV and radio stations and social media platforms. They fund political parties and pay for political ads that overwhelm our thinking with the drumbeat that we need to cut “our” high taxes and that we must forever keep finding ways to do less with less. 
If you’re eligible to vote but not sure you are registered, call your friendly town clerk and find out. It’s a miracle of Vermont law that you can register and vote even on Election Day — though your hardworking clerk will appreciate you not waiting that long. Don’t miss this chance to change the failing status quo.
Alan Turnbull
Craftsbury, Vt.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Tax the rich to spare the rest of us.

name: California
title: How Prop 45 could reshape California’s fight over data centers
text:
In summary
Prop. 45, billed as a pro-housing development measure, may have the unintended consequence of making it easier to build data centers, opponents say.




California voters considering Proposition 45 will decide the fate of a sweeping infrastructure measure that opponents warn could render the state’s brand-new data center laws virtually toothless.
That would make it far easier for developers to force unwanted facilities into local communities, potentially undermining a growing wave of bans, moratoriums, and anti-data-center resolutions at the city and county level.
Data center backers insist the ballot measure will do nothing for them — even as some data center beneficiaries are spending big backing Prop. 45.
Supporters have framed Prop. 45 as a tool to accelerate critical infrastructure projects, like housing and schools and the measure does not directly name data centers among the sorts of projects it considers critical. But some legal scholars and environmental advocates say that the proposition’s technical language creates a loophole. By expediting environmental reviews under the California Environmental Quality Act for broad categories of projects — including broadband internet facilities and any additional infrastructure required to get them up and running — the measure could quietly allow data centers to bypass recent state safeguards and local scrutiny.
Julia Stein, a legal scholar and deputy director at UCLA School of Law’s Emmett Institute on Climate Change and the Environment, warns that the measure acts as a “blunt force instrument when it comes to streamlining” because of how wide its secondary umbrella extends.
“What Prop. 45 does is designate an entire class of projects that would be subject to streamlining, and then it also says that projects ancillary to those projects — so something that you might need to do in the course of the development of the project that’s exempted itself — would fall within that same streamlining bubble,” Stein said. 
Telecommunications projects are explicitly streamlined under the proposition, “and there’s an argument that the development of data centers might be necessary for projects like that,” Stein added.
Other projects, like high-speed rail, are explicitly excluded from streamlining under the proposition — but data centers are not on that list, either. Stein and three other environmental law scholars told CalMatters that this opens the door for legal challenges.
“The fact that they excluded some projects but have not expressly excluded data centers, a court would probably actually interpret that not as an unintentional oversight, but rather as intent to include data centers in the initiative,” said Matt McKerley, an attorney with Shute, Mihaly and Weinberger. 
Further, opponents argue that the proposition’s language, which includes a clause that it would supersede other related laws, would override measures like the recently-passed Senate Bill 887, which made it harder to fast-track environmental review for data centers.
Industry representatives say these objections to Prop. 45 are misplaced. The Data Center Coalition, an industry group supporting Prop. 45, insists their facilities fall outside the initiative’s scope, which focuses largely on housing development.
“The Data Center Coalition has reviewed Proposition 45 and concluded that data centers are not eligible for Prop. 45’s streamlining, nor are they a covered entity under any part of the measure,” said Khara Boender, the coalition’s Director of Government Affairs—West.
Industry representatives also point to a recent legal opinion memo from California’s Office of Legislative Counsel, which provides legal services to members of the Legislature. The memo argues that Prop. 45’s statutory definitions do not apply to data centers.
Despite maintaining that data centers fall outside the proposition’s reach, tech and utility interests benefiting from California’s computing boom are putting massive financial weight behind its passage. Corporate backers have poured over $10 million into the Yes on Prop. 45 campaign, including $3.05 million from utility giant PG&E and $500,000 from warehouse and data center developer Prologis — a cash influx that opponents argue reveals who truly expects to profit if the measure passes. 
The debate over Prop. 45’s data center impact comes at a pivotal moment in California’s AI infrastructure boom. Gov. Gavin Newsom recently signed seven landmark data center laws aimed at forcing operators to disclose water usage, pay for their own grid upgrades, and undergo environmental review.
Yet local communities aren’t waiting for state regulations to take effect. Amid rising fears of rate hikes, grid overload, and water depletion, grassroots opposition has erupted across California. At least 26 cities and counties have proposed or passed moratoriums, bans, or strict limits aimed to stop data center development in their communities.
Nina Robertson, a deputy managing attorney in Earthjustice’s California regional office, said the ambiguity written into the ballot text would trigger immediate legal battles over local permitting authority.
“And who’s going to bear the cost of that litigation?” Robertson asked. “It’s going to be the local governments.”

name: California
title: California can’t afford to keep Prop 13 loopholes open when billions of dollars are on the line
text:
Guest Commentary written by

John Kim
John Kim is the president and CEO of Catalyst California.


I have fond memories of growing up in the suburbs of Los Angeles in the 1970s. The weather felt perfect. Yes, there were hot days, but you could look forward to perfect summer nights. Public schools felt relatively new, which they were, and there were open spaces yet to be explored. 
Though there was a new danger every week on the news, I somehow felt safe tumbling around, untethered, in the back of my parents’ station wagon. 
The state’s transformation over the last 50 years has been mind boggling. You likely would have been laughed out of most rooms in the ‘70s for predicting that California would become the fourth-largest economy on earth, behind only the United States, China and Germany. 
Innovations forged here reshaped how the world works. And yet, state and local governments failed to keep up.
The population nearly doubled, but we did too little to house these new Californians. We made some gains in public schools after short-sighted disinvestment during the 1980s and ‘90s, but we still struggle with achievement gaps across race and class.
We set conditions for technological invention but do too little to mitigate an exploding wealth gap that would make the Gilded Age blush. And we’re nowhere near ready to manage an AI-driven economic transition, let alone the increasing severity and cadence of climate catastrophes. 
The favorite bogeyman, though, is bureaucratic intransigence, sometimes called one-party rule. But we should be clear the problem isn’t partisanship or a lack of imagination — it’s structural and goes back to the 1970s. 
Proposition 13 was sold in 1978 as a way to save grandma’s house from unpredictable property tax bills. It also became a permanent discount for wealthy, corporate property owners. 
Under the proposition, homeowners pay taxes based on market value when they bought their homes, rather than on current values. And that’s fine. But since Prop 13 passed, high-priced tax attorneys have leveraged loopholes in Prop. 13 to let commercial and industrial property owners avoid property reassessments and higher taxes when their property changes hands. 
The result: billions of dollars in lost tax revenue.
USC researchers recently estimated that as much as $25.1 billion more could be collected per year by state and local governments if California closes Prop. 13’s commercial and industrial loophole and those properties are assessed at their current fair-market values.
Think of all we could do with those resources if we told wealthy corporations, after 50 years, that the party’s over.
California is about to need every dollar it can raise. 
President Donald Trump’s signature legislation, dubbed the One Big Beautiful Bill, takes healthcare and food aid from working families and hands the money to the wealthiest Americans.
Roughly 2 million Californians will fall off Medi-Cal by 2028, and nearly half a million are now being shoved off CalFresh. The state now has to cover a deficit of more than $20 billion a year.
And again public school districts up and down the state are struggling with empty coffers and potential layoffs.
Often big wins get lost in a bureaucratic wilderness, and cynicism rises among voters who are legitimately hurting.
But when we focus, we can get it right — like when the state offered all 4-year-olds an extra year of education by adding transitional kindergarten to public schools. This is a concrete, visionary program that protects the pocketbooks of California families while increasing trust in government.  
Now the Legislature and next governor have a rare political window. They can refill the federal breach and create a version of government we all want and need. The goal is not to restore California to 1970, but to build what will get us to 2070.
Until they seize this chance, the whole state is like me as a kid in the back of that station wagon: No seat belt. No headrest. Nothing to hold on to. 
Just sliding around, bracing for whatever comes next.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT will pay you to beat New York in court. Almost no one can collect.
text:
Last July, Connecticut passed a law that reads like a dare. 
Public Act 25-172 promises a Connecticut resident who pays New York income tax on days worked at home in Connecticut a credit equal to 60 percent of the extra Connecticut tax that results when the state recalculates the credit it gave for that New York tax. 
The act also waives penalties and interest on the late Connecticut tax. It reaches back to tax years beginning in 2020.
The target is New York’s convenience-of-the-employer rule. One sentence of New York regulation says a nonresident’s days worked outside New York count as New York days unless the work was done out of state “of necessity, as distinguished from convenience.” New York’s 2006 guidance confines the rule to employees whose primary office is in New York and excuses a home day only when the home is a “bona fide employer office.” A Connecticut resident with a Manhattan employer who works Fridays in Fairfield pays New York tax on Friday.
To collect Connecticut’s 60 percent, the resident must do four things, and the act joins them with “and.” Pay the New York tax. Apply to New York for a refund and be denied. Appeal that denial to a court or tribunal. Obtain a final decision ordering New York to refund the tax.
On July 2, the Appellate Division, Third Department, the court that hears appeals from New York’s Tax Appeals Tribunal, ruled against Edward Zelinsky, a Connecticut resident and law professor who has been fighting this rule since his first Tribunal decision in 2001. The Tribunal had ruled against him in May 2025. The court found “no constitutional or other infirmity” in the rule, said the debate over remote work “remain[s] the province of the Legislature,” and saw “no basis to disturb the Tribunal’s determination sustaining the taxation.” The one road the act requires a resident to travel, denial, appeal, and a final win, was just closed again by the court at the end of it. As far as I can find, nobody has yet qualified for the credit, and after July no one is likely to.
There is a second problem, and it is Connecticut’s own. 
Since tax years beginning in 2019, Connecticut has had the same rule. Section 12-711 of the General Statutes counts as Connecticut income the pay of a nonresident for “days worked outside this state for such person’s convenience if such person’s state of domicile uses a similar test.” The Department of Revenue Services says plainly that for a New York resident working from home for a Connecticut employer, “Connecticut will apply the New York ‘convenience of the employer’ test.” 
Connecticut taxes New Yorkers at home in New York exactly as New York taxes Connecticut residents at home in Connecticut. The act pays Connecticut residents to attack, in New York’s courts, a rule Connecticut keeps on its own books.
What actually protects a Connecticut commuter is older and duller than the bounty. Section 12-704 gives residents a credit for income tax paid to another state, claimed on Schedule 2 of the CT-1040. The instructions to that form define qualifying income to include compensation “for personal services performed from a home office in Connecticut for an employer in a qualifying jurisdiction that applies a convenience of the employer test.” 
In plain terms: Connecticut already credits the New York tax on those Fridays. The credit is capped at the share of Connecticut tax that the New York income represents, and it cannot push Connecticut tax below what would be due if the New York income were left out, so a resident still pays the difference where New York’s tax runs higher. But the resident is not taxed twice on the same wage. The commuter who files Schedule 2 correctly and attaches the New York return, as Connecticut requires, is made whole to the extent Connecticut law allows, with no lawsuit.
If the General Assembly believes the convenience rule is unjust, it has two honest options. It can repeal Connecticut’s mirror of the rule, which would cost the state revenue from New Yorkers and would at least match its words to its conduct. Or it can pursue what no two of New York, New Jersey and Connecticut have ever signed: a reciprocal agreement. New Jersey’s only such agreement, with Pennsylvania, covers wages and nothing else. A bounty for winning a case the courts have now rejected three times is neither.
In the meantime, Connecticut residents with New York offices should do three things this filing season. Keep a day log; New York audits these. Ask the employer, in writing, whether the home office meets New York’s bona fide employer office test. And claim the Schedule 2 credit, with the New York return attached. The remedy is already in the instructions.
Myung Keon Kim is a certified public accountant licensed in New York whose practice prepares New York, New Jersey and Connecticut returns for individuals and small businesses.

name: Mississippi Today
title: The false promise of consolidation in West Bolivar schools: ‘It takes a toll’
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
SHAW — Cassandra Phillips hates to see the old Ray Brooks School building rotting off Highway 1. 
To local lawmakers and residents, it was the best maintained public schoolhouse in Bolivar County. The one structure connected to a gymnasium with a vaulted ceiling and glossy wooden floors and a cafeteria with cushioned booths in maraschino red.
Now, vines hang where school banners did. Shelves and desks lie rusted and mangled in the abandoned breezeway, and wires stripped of their copper lay limp from behind shattered doors and windows.
Ray Brooks School is pictured in Benoit on Friday, September 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
The Ray Brooks School, which served grades K-12, was a casualty of a 2014 consolidation between Benoit’s school district and those in Rosedale and Shaw. 
But the community lost more than a school. Families had gathered at the building for repasts, impromptu kickball tournaments and youth mentoring. They could attend a football game or pick up a child without making a 20-minute drive — the typical amount of time it takes now to get to school in Shaw. 
Now, former Ray Brooks Tigers, including Phillips, cheer for the Shaw Warriors, their pre-consolidation rivals. But that harmony that took six years to achieve is at risk again.
Ja’khyria Williams, from left, Zalia Sanders and Cassandra Phillips talk about Shaw High School during the school’s football game against Leland at Shaw’s former high school football stadium on Friday, Sept. 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
State lawmakers are considering another consolidation in Bolivar County, which has three districts: North Bolivar, West Bolivar and Cleveland. The details of lawmakers’ new consolidation plans are not yet clear, and  the promises of cost savings and better schools from the last one have fallen far short of expectations. Schools have closed, buildings have deteriorated and turmoil has plagued the resulting district. 
“Benoit has lost so much,” Phillips said.
Taking the fight against consolidation to Jackson
In January 2012, Beverly Culley, Benoit’s superintendent, addressed lawmakers to argue against consolidation. She handed packets detailing district budgets and student test scores.
She brought students, too. They sang a hymn. She made an impassioned speech and listed off the district’s high test scores relative to its neighbors. Benoit was one of the best performing school districts in the Mississippi Delta. The district had minimal debt. The community needed its schools.
“They didn’t listen,” Culley said. “They had all the data. But none of that mattered because they were going to do what they were going to do.”
Evelyn Henry, who served on the Shaw school board before the consolidation, was also present that session, but with a different pitch. She presented a binder with the total cost of unaddressed maintenance issues in Shaw schools, which was steep, she recalled. 
Ray Brooks School is pictured in Benoit on Friday, September 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayRay Brooks School is pictured in Benoit on Friday, September 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayRay Brooks School is pictured in Benoit on Friday, September 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayRay Brooks School is pictured in Benoit on Friday, September 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayRay Brooks School is pictured in Benoit on Friday, September 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayThe old library at Ray Brooks School is pictured in Benoit on Friday, September 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayRay Brooks School is pictured in Benoit on Friday, September 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
She hoped if lawmakers did go through with consolidation, they would consider consolidation with Cleveland, which had a larger tax base and was closer in distance.
“We had to realize something was going to happen,” Henry said of the board’s attempt to negotiate. “I just wish we could have had somebody to help us before we went to Jackson so we looked like a unified front.”
Neither Culley or Henry’s wishes were honored, both now saying their fears were realized.
‘We just couldn’t sit down and just make it work’
The consolidated West Bolivar school board would be tasked with fixing crumbling infrastructure in Rosedale and Shaw with little money. Lawmakers chose three communities with some of the lowest tax bases in the state to combine, which Henry felt set them up for failure.
The consolidated districts saved roughly $400,000 in administrative costs, much less than lawmakers’ claims the move would save up to  $1.6 million.
Jackie Lloyd, who has represented Rosedale schools on the West Bolivar board since consolidation, recalled getting little technical assistance from the state Education Department after the districts merged. She said pooling the different schools’ resources and then dispersing them equitably was particularly challenging.
Joyce Brown, left, and Shelia Ratliff prepare for Leland and Shaw high schools’ football game at Shaw’s former high school football stadium on Friday, Sept. 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
The districts had a combined $1.48 million in debt coming into the consolidation. West Bolivar School District, based in Rosedale, owed more than $1 million. Benoit’s district only owed $40,000.
Henry, who represented Shaw on the consolidated school board until 2020, had the same observation as Lloyd. She felt each community’s representatives were only interested in measures that would benefit their schools. The board increasingly failed to reach consensus, and gridlock on votes became common.
Five years and four superintendents later, Henry observed a more aggressive school board whose actions were fueled by the increasing polarization. According to a 2020 lawsuit Culley filed against the district and board members, board members aggressively bullied and harassed her. She alleged the behavior started soon after she was appointed superintendent of the consolidated district in 2017.
The district settled out of court in 2020 for an undisclosed amount for alleged behavior that U.S. District Court Judge Michal P. Mills called “distasteful.”
In Shaw, district consolidation meant no high school, no band
While videos of board members’ quarrels reached viewers on Facebook, district infrastructure continued to crumble. Two district high school buildings were eventually condemned: Shaw in 2018 and West Bolivar in Rosedale in 2020. As a result, Shaw High students attend classes at the elementary school building.
For Shelia Ratliffe, a Shaw alum, budget cuts at the school mean her children missed out on extracurriculars. 
At the Sept. 14 football game, Ratliffe pointed to the old Shaw High school gym, where she remembered majorette and band practices took place. She remembered the pride the community felt for Shaw’s band, when they had one.
The old gymnasium at the former Shaw High School is pictured in Shaw on Friday, Sept. 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Failing infrastructure and fewer extracurricular offerings weren’t inevitable, Henry said. The Shaw school board received a grant from the Mississippi Department of Archives and History to renovate the high school building prior to consolidation. A crew from Jackson provided an on-site inspection along with a project overview in 2013, she recalled.
Later, the consolidated school board and a series of superintendents never prioritized the project. Instead, they abandoned the historic high school and relocated its students to the McEvans Elementary building.
Karmenisha Moore, left, and Jarquez Moore talk about school consolidation and the football game between Shaw and Leland in Shaw on Friday, September 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayCora Jackson talks about Delta Hands for Hope in Shaw on Friday, September 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayCora sits at a table at Delta Hands for Hope in Shaw on Friday, September 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayDebbie Brooks talks about her efforts while working with Delta Hands for Hope in Shaw on Friday, September 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayCora Jackson gives a tour of Delta Hands for Hope in Shaw on Friday, September 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayDonated computers are in place at Delta Hands for Hope in Shaw on Friday, September 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayCora Jackson talks about the books donated to Delta Hands for Hope while giving a tour of the nonprofit organization in Shaw on Friday, September 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayKarmenisha Moore, left, and Jarquez Moore talk about school consolidation and the football game between Shaw and Leland in Shaw on Friday, September 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
In 2020, the West Bolivar Consolidated school board, now dominated by representatives from Shaw and Rosedale — and one from Benoit — voted to close Ray Brooks, too.
“It made no sense,” Culley, the former Benoit superintendent, recalled. 
The district installed two portable toilets by the concession stand for spectators and players alike in lieu of a field house at Shaw High’s football field. 
Portable toilets are in place for Leland and Shaw high schools’ football game at Shaw’s former high school football stadium on Friday, Sept. 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
“Our community, Shaw, just really started feeling like the ugly child,” said Henry of upkeep projects that went ignored at her alma mater. She said she paid for McEvans school sign out of pocket to replace an old, decrepit one, and the board moved slowly on other Shaw priorities. 
Communities adjust to playing on the same team 
Zalia Sanders, a Benoit native and a senior at Shaw High, was miles away from home at the Aug. 28 matchup between Leland and Shaw. But the rural community on a bayou has become a second home for her. She, along with three other students, said Shaw and Benoit have come together despite a tumultuous consolidation in 2014.
Leland cheerleaders perform on the sidelines during their school’s football game against Shaw High School at Shaw’s former high school football stadium on Friday, Sept. 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayLeland plays against Shaw High School at Shaw’s former high school football stadium on Friday, Sept. 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayShaw players celebrate a play during their game against Leland at Shaw’s former high school football stadium on Friday, Sept. 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayA Leland player runs the ball during their game against Shaw at Shaw’s former high school football stadium on Friday, Sept. 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayA Shaw player runs the ball during their game against Leland at Shaw’s former high school football stadium on Friday, Sept. 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayA Shaw player runs the ball during their game against Leland at Shaw’s former high school football stadium on Friday, Sept. 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayShaw High School cheerleaders pose for a photo before players take the field against Leland at Shaw’s former high school football stadium on Friday, Sept. 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
At the game, she stood by the fence with her older sister, Ja’khyria Williams, who is a college freshman. They reflected on what became common in the wake of consolidation: student fights.
She said the rivalry between Rosedale and her native Benoit can be fierce — a  feud that stretches back to the 1980s, long before her time in school. 
There was an uptick in fighting between Rosedale and Shaw youth in the years after the consolidation in the late 2010s and in 2024, Rosedale Police Chief Aaron Malone recalled. But while he remembers some dispatches last year related to disputes, this year has been mostly quiet.
The catalyst can be as small as an unfriendly look or as big as allegations of romantic infidelity, Sanders said. 
Shaw fans cheer after a play during their game against Leland at Shaw’s former high school football stadium on Friday, Sept. 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Still, she said, she loves Shaw High. She got more comfortable at Shaw schools through joining the volleyball team, she says. 
“When you’re playing on the same team, you get to know each other as people.”
Shaw, the town miles down the country highway, no longer feels so foreign, she said. But between board members weighing another school closure and consolidation talk in Jackson, students like her might be sent to yet another community for school.
Shaw residents don’t want to reopen the wounds of consolidation
Arika Williams, a Benoit native, was wrapping up her shift in the concession stand.
By the fourth quarter, she was counting cash from the stand’s register beneath the hum of an electronic fan. Her brows knitted beneath her tortoiseshell-framed eyeglasses as she shifted to counting the remaining stock of chips and sodas.
Arika Williams works the concession stand during Shaw High School’s football game against Leland at Shaw’s former high school football stadium on Friday, Sept. 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
“If we can all work together and go in the direction we’re going, I think we can all be successful,” Williams said. Initially, she worried consolidation could mean her son would miss out on extracurricular opportunities in Shaw and spend too much time on a school bus.
The big Delta sky had gone black by the fourth quarter. The headlights of old Silverados lit up reflective workmans’ vests in the dark streets by the field. Some were trying to catch the game’s last moments after getting off work.
In the past, some of the Shaw Warriors’ biggest boosters were Ray Brooks Tigers. Ray Brooks alumni, Lajaruis Jaron among them, said they know the importance of community more than anyone in the county. They know how losing schools and football victories can fracture a community. 
During the football game, he leaned forward to watch a Warrior nab the ball. He cheered. The player ran the ball to the end zone. Two students sprinted school flags by the edges of the field. 
Shaw scored again.
Leland fans watch as players compete against Shaw High School at Shaw’s former high school football stadium on Friday, Sept. 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Jarone said he attends each season’s game whether home or away. He owns multiple maroon and yellow T-shirts. He couldn’t imagine autumn without a Warriors football game. 
“When the bus moves, I move,” he said.
Jarone attended Ray Brooks School, not Shaw, but like Williams and Phillips and Sanders, he said he’s found a new home. He’d hate for another district consolidation to force students to find another one.
“I hope consolidation doesn’t happen to these kids like it did to us because it will take a toll,” he said. “This is how it’s always been for small communities. The odds have always been stacked against us.”

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Commentary: Are sales taxes the fairest way to fund improved schools? 47 localities are asking voters to decide.
text:
A view from outside the newly renovated Gloucester County High School, which opened last September. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury)Amid lingering inflation from high fuel prices, 47 Virginia localities are about to ask their residents to vote on Tuesday for a ballot question that will make every retail purchase they make near their homes costlier.
Interesting timing to say the least. But that doesn’t make it wrong.
If voters approve the proposed tax increases, which are capped at 1%, their proceeds would by law be directed toward capital improvements for public schools in those localities. That’s a worthy purpose, ranking right up there with public safety and healthcare.
Yet the decision is not easy. Voters are being asked to weigh their current financial situations against their children’s futures. There are valid points on either side of this argument that warrant respect.
Still, it’s hard not to feel it’s a shame that it’s come to this.
Virginia localities weigh 1% sales tax for school construction as voters decide on expansion

The sales tax is the most regressive form of taxation there is, burdening most those who have the least. 
The person who works all day then moonlights as a rideshare driver to cover rent, grocery and utility bills with no capacity to save anything pays as much tax on a new refrigerator as a Fortune 500 CEO with a summer house on Martha’s Vineyard and a fleet of Teslas.
It’s a shame because as a commonwealth, our state leaders have preened and posed and positioned themselves as champions of making our schools — in affluent communities and poor ones — safe, modern and excellent, turning out graduates who can hold their own anywhere. You know, the literal definition of a “commonwealth.”
But in the end, the full measure of K-12 educational excellence was tossed back into the laps of Virginia’s 133 localities. 
Because Virginia is a Dillon Rule state — meaning local governments are strictly limited in the tax rates they can raise without legislative approval — the General Assembly empowered the 95 counties and 38 independent cities to ask their voters if they will shoulder a sales tax boost. Thirty-five percent of those localities are doing that in this election.
State approval didn’t happen through the more transparent regular legislative process. A stand-alone bill that would have authorized the extra penny of tax on every dollar’s worth of retail spending passed the House of Delegates this year, but the Senate carried it over to the 2027 session.
The authorization was buried in small type and dense legislative jargon on page 723 of the 887-page state budget enacted on June 29, one day ahead of the deadline for averting a state government shutdown.
Eight Virginia localities — Charlotte, Gloucester, Halifax, Henry, Northampton, Patrick and Pittsylvania counties and the city of Danville — got state permission to ask their voters to approve the sales tax increase before it was extended to all localities this year.
As the Mercury’s Nathaniel Cline explained in his reporting on Oct. 5, those eight localities have generated a combined $119 million through those higher taxes since 2019, but results are mixed and satisfaction is not universal.
In Halifax, the first locality to receive authorization, students enjoy a new high school and remodeled elementary and middle schools that wouldn’t have been affordable without the $20.8 million the county has taken in over the past five years.
Danville took in nearly $31 million from 2023 through last year, giving the city ample bonding authority for impressive upgrades to its facilities.
That’s not bringing much comfort, however, to voters in York County, which would see its combined sales tax rate reach 8% — the highest in Virginia — if the measure passes. Already, York is tied with two of its Peninsula neighbors, James City County and Williamsburg, for the state’s highest rate at 7%.
By no stretch is York County struggling economically. According to the Census Bureau’s American Community Survey, its median annual household income is just under $110,000, or about $16,800 greater than the statewide median. 
But that doesn’t translate to York residents gladly paying significantly more in taxes on their purchases than the statewide average of just under 6%.
York County Supervisor G. Stephen Roane Jr. opposed putting the sales tax increase measure on the countywide ballot with so little time to weigh the political and economic consequences against the benefits.
“I thought we needed time to study other options to seek money to provide for school infrastructure projects. I thought we moved too quickly,” he said in an interview.
Particularly, he said, he was concerned about the effect the state’s highest sales tax could have on merchants in his county. Within reason, consumers will travel to save money, and retailers in the cities of Poquoson and Hampton — both sharing York’s eastern boundary — could beckon frugal York shoppers to make the short drive and exploit a tax rate two percentage points lower, especially on big-ticket items.
As incomes go, York’s ranking among the top 10% of the state’s most affluent localities can be quite misleading, Roane noted.
“Affluence is an average across the board, so there are people below that average who are going to struggle,” he said. “You’ve got to be mindful of everybody in the county.”
Virginia as a whole compares favorably to neighboring states when it comes to sales tax burdens. Our average combined state and local rates are about even with those of every adjacent state but Tennessee — a state that proudly eschews an income tax yet forces consumers to pay almost an extra dime on every retail dollar spent except for groceries, which are taxed at a lower rate.
Even with the additional penny of sales taxes for schools, Virginia would still be a bargain compared to Tennessee and wouldn’t make the commonwealth inherently uncompetitive with any other nextdoor state.
The greater question for Virginians heading to the polls, however, is whether this is the most equitable way to invest in our local public schools and, by extension, the commonwealth’s future.
Fortunately, these are the most meaningful and productive questions that we as a commonwealth can and should ask ourselves — at all levels of government. And in the end, there are good answers and better answers, but no wrong ones.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Mixed reactions among disabled Granite Staters on the CFI lawsuit settlement
text:
Kathy Bates, Jim and Pat Piet and Dan Hebert, shown here in their respective homes, each receive services to help them perform the daily activities of life with their disability through New Hampshire's Choices for Independence program. A class action lawsuit over the program's inadequacies was settled earlier this month. (Photos by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)Kathy Bates was elated when she heard that her attorneys and the state of New Hampshire settled a yearslong lawsuit over the Medicaid program that she relies on for care.
Husband and wife duo Jim and Pat Piet are more skeptical and fear that this settlement alone won’t fix the lackluster program without harming other programs.
Dan Hebert, on the other hand, is cautiously optimistic. He sees the potential for big upside, but he also sees pitfalls.
 
Proposed Class Action Settlement For Fitzmorris v DHHS 

Bates, Piet and Hebert are all participants in New Hampshire’s Choices for Independence, a state-run Medicaid program that provides in-home care to people with disabilities and older adults. The goal of the program is to allow them to stay in their own home by hiring caregivers and other supports to avoid a nursing home, something that even the state acknowledges would cost roughly three times as much money.
After years of severe underinvestment in the program, a coalition of nonprofits focused on disability and elderly rights sued the state, arguing that by not properly funding the program the state was at risk of illegally institutionalizing people with disabilities. The case, which lasted almost six years and became a class action lawsuit, was set to go to trial next month before both sides came to an agreement to settle the case earlier this month.
The settlement still must be approved by federal Judge Paul Barbadoro, but class members like Bates, Piet and Hebert have all had a chance to review the settlement, which has major implications on their daily lives.
Elation
Bates is a named plaintiff in the suit. That means she’s been involved in the case since its earliest days and was a representative for the whole class.
“I’m really glad we got here,” she said, before joking, “I probably would’ve said no if I realized it would’ve taken this long.”
Bates, who lives in Somersworth, has cerebral palsy. In 2021, she and three other CFI participants represented by the AARP Foundation, the Disability Rights Center of New Hampshire, New Hampshire Legal Assistance and Nixon Peabody sued the state over the program. Soon after, the case became a class action and grew to encompass the thousands of New Hampshire residents in the CFI program. Bates said she’s relieved the case, which was time-consuming and draining, is over.
Kathy Bates poses for a photo in her Somersworth home on March 25, 2025. Bates said having aides help her with everyday tasks allows her to do fulfilling advocacy work. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)
“It feels like it was a part-time job,” she said.  
Core to the plaintiffs’ arguments was that CFI participants weren’t getting the services the state had approved them for. Because of underfunding, CFI participants have long reported, wages were so low that hiring caregivers is near impossible. Vacancies mean shifts go unworked and CFI participants don’t get the help they need to do basic activities of living like getting out of bed, dressing themselves, showering, cooking meals and cleaning. This, their attorneys argued, was putting CFI participants at risk of being put in an institution, a violation of their rights under the 1990 Americans with Disabilities Act and the 1973 Rehabilitation Act. To settle the lawsuit and avert a trial, the state agreed to take a series of steps aimed at solving the issue:

The Department of Health and Human Services agreed to hire a third-party consultant to analyze the state’s network of caregivers to determine whether it meets the needs of the participants. Specifically, the consultant must identify the level of service the state approved for participants versus how much they actually received.
DHHS also agreed to ensure every participant has a contingency plan in place should they not receive their approved services and to execute that plan for any participants who received less than 50% of their approved services each month.
Reimbursement rates set by the state determine caregiver salaries. DHHS agreed to perform an analysis on its reimbursement rates.
DHHS also agreed to ask state lawmakers for biennial reimbursement rate increases to match inflation.
DHHS agreed to expand use of “specialized rates” given to participants who struggle to hire aides.
DHHS agreed to create an online portal and directory of caregivers.
Finally, DHHS agreed to expand its existing grievance system to allow complaints about missed services.
Twice a year, DHHS would be required to create a report outlining its compliance with the agreement.

Bates said the part she’s most excited for is the registry of caregivers. She’s long complained about how challenging it is to hire aides. Bate hires them herself and the caregivers are paid by a third party agency using state funds. She currently uses Craig’s List ads and staffing agencies to find caregivers but is excited to have a new tool she hopes will be more effective. Most of all she’s excited about what it means for the people that help her get out of bed in the morning, people she’s really grateful for.
She hopes “it’ll make the profession of caregiving and the people who do this work” more respected. She explained that lots of her caregivers are single mothers trying to support their own families in addition to supporting her.
“If they make more money in the profession, it becomes a real career option,” she said. “It’ll make life easier for them.”
The New Hampshire Department of Health and Human Services, photographed here on Oct. 19, 2026, operates Medicaid in New Hampshire, which encompasses several different programs aimed at supporting people with disabilities in addition to providing low-income Granite Staters with health coverage. The department has agreed to a series of changes to its Choices for Independence Program in exchange for settling a class action lawsuit and . (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)
She knows, however, that change will take time.
“I guess I’ll just have to be patient,” she said.
Skepticism
When Pat Vincent-Piet first heard about the settlement, her first question was “like everything, who pays for this again?”
In a class action lawsuit where the plaintiffs’ attorneys represent thousands of people in one suit, complete agreement among class members is very rare.
Pat and Jim Piet live in Concord and both have cerebral palsy. However, cerebral palsy, like many disabilities, has a spectrum of symptoms. Pat does not need the same level of care as Jim, who uses a wheelchair and has caregivers help him perform many of the daily activities of life.
The couple is skeptical. The settlement doesn’t commit the state to spending more money on the program, which would be needed to raise caregiver salaries and ensure all services are provided. It merely instructs DHHS to ask lawmakers to increase funding to match inflation and create reports about the program. The plaintiffs’ attorneys hope the reports demonstrate the dire needs of this program and convince lawmakers to properly fund the program, but DHHS can’t force lawmakers to give it additional funding. And the reports mandated by the settlement do not have to be produced until after the Legislature commences its budget-making process early next year.
“The only way that works is if we take some money from someone else.” Pat said.
Pat is concerned that to fix one Medicaid program, DHHS will have to raid the coffers of another, such as the developmental disability waiver, another Medicaid program that supports people with intellectual and developmental disabilities rather than purely physical ones. She has little confidence the Legislature will give DHHS the funding needed to reform CFI. She pointed to recent cuts to the Medicaid program over the past two years.
Jim and Pat Piet pose for a photo in their Concord home. The couple said that hiring aides to help Jim with everyday tasks in light of his cerebral palsy is “damn near impossible.” (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)
Medicaid, which is run jointly by states and the federal government, encompasses several programs. In addition to the several that support people with various disabilities, traditional Medicaid offers health coverage to low-income Americans. In 2025, Congress passed a law that KFF estimated will cut $991 billion from Medicaid nationwide. That same year, New Hampshire lawmakers implemented multiple cost-saving measures on the state level. They are set to begin charging premiums to certain traditional Medicaid recipients soon and have decreased the amount of prescription costs the state will cover. Pat argues “all of those things are connected.”
Jim and Pat also questioned whether the state has the staff to create these reports and do the extra work this settlement requires. They said the Medicaid personnel they interact with to get reapproved for services every year and complete other bureaucratic tasks tell them they’re too understaffed to get the work they currently have on their plate done.
“There’s no one to implement these requirements,” Jim said.
Jim and Pat feel they’re luckier than most CFI participants. When they can’t find a caregiver to cover a shift, Pat steps in to help. Single participants don’t have that luxury. Still, Jim wants his wife to be his wife, not his aide. It’s also hindered Pat’s career and her ability to earn a living, pay taxes and contribute to the community.
Cautious optimism
Dan Hebert, who also lives in Concord, had dates set on his calendar for a potential trial and was surprised to learn about the settlement. His takeaway is cautious optimism.
What he likes about the settlement: “a greater push toward transparency” and “what’s hopefully going to be an increase in compensation for the caregivers.”
The class action lawsuit, entitled Fitzmorris v DHHS, was being litigated in the U.S. District Court of New Hampshire, photographed here on Aug. 27, 2025. The case narrowly averted a trial, planned for November, when the parties reached a settlement agreement in early October. (Photo by Ethan DeWitt/New Hampshire Bulletin)
Hebert agrees with the attorneys’ argument that demonstrating the lackluster nature of CFI could push lawmakers to better fund it.
“I counted no less than five reports that are mandated in this,” he said. “And while the department has had this information already, having it in five reports transparently and announced means that everyone sees it upfront and it’s readable. I think that’s important.”
He’s also planning to utilize the grievance system.
“I can’t tell you that it’s going to work,” he said. “I can’t tell you that it’s not going to work. I don’t know, but I do know that the monitoring is going to tell us the truth, and we’re all going to see it.”
Hebert is disappointed the reports won’t be ready before state lawmakers begin budget deliberations as this likely pushes back any real fiscal solution to the problems CFI faces until 2029, the following budget year. He wishes this could be solved sooner.
Dan Hebert, photographed here in his Concord home on Nov. 3, 2025, is one of the CFI participants involved in a lawsuit against the state. He’s hopeful the settlement will be enough to fix the lackluster program. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)
Overall, he said he’s happy the settlement was struck.
“I think that the attorneys that we have negotiated this settlement to try to do the best that they could,” he said. “And if this is what we’re gonna try, I’m optimistic.”
The Disability Rights Centers, one of the organizations litigating the case, is holding two webinars to inform CFI participants about the settlement on Nov. 17 at 10 a.m and Nov. 30 at 6 p.m. More details are available online at https://cfi.drcnh.org.
Any class member that objects to the settlement can have their voice heard in court on Jan. 21 at the U.S. District Court in Concord. They can also mail in their written complaints by Dec. 7 with the U.S. District Court at 55 Pleasant St. in Concord, NH (ZIP code 03301). Barbadoro, the judge, will decide whether to approve the settlement soon after.
Meanwhile, Hebert still relies on family and friends to help him out because he can’t find enough professional caregivers willing to work for the rates CFI offers.
“My world hasn’t changed today,” Hebert said. “But I’m hoping that it will.”

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Can Ron DeSantis push Amendment 3 over the top?
text:
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis speaking the USF Health Morsani Center for Advanced Healthcare in Tampa on June 25, 2025. (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix)Ron DeSantis was in Crystal River Wednesday, ostensibly to announce that his administration was providing an additional $100 million to restore and protect Florida’s water resources across 45 projects.
However, he spent nearly half of his press conference making the case once again for Amendment 3, the proposal on the statewide ballot that would cut property taxes for Florida homeowners.
With six days to go before Election Day, polls indicate the proposal might be in danger of failing.
A St. Pete Polls survey released Wednesday shows the measure with 44% support, with 39% opposed and 17% unsure. A University of North Florida poll released last week found Amendment 3 getting 50% support. Both would fall far short of the 60% threshold required for passage.
Although the governor has been the main driving force for well over a year-and-a-half in placing the property tax cut proposal before the voters, he initially declined to campaign for it after the Republican-controlled Legislature in June enacted changes to his original language.
He has since reversed that stance and has been actively supporting it, although not in any campaign ads. On Monday, he held a roundtable discussion with U.S. Sen. Ashley Moody and Department of Agriculture Commissioner Wilton Simpson to extoll the proposal’s virtues and praised it again Wednesday as his press conference aired on the Florida Channel.
A variety of organizations have strongly opposed the measure, fearing it would significantly reduce tax revenues for local governments, forcing them to make serious budget cuts. State economists have estimated Amendment 3 would reduce revenue by $5 billion in its first year and as much as $12 billion annually when fully implemented.
The governor made the case in Crystal River that local governments can afford to take a financial haircut, noting they took in $32 billion in property tax revenues in 2019 and now receive $62 billion, well above what he says the pace of inflation and population growth would justify.
“My question is for those who say that we won’t have any services if Amendment 3 passes, did we not have services in 2019?” DeSantis asked. “So, don’t tell me we can’t give our homesteaders a relief. We can do it. One hundred percent.”
Law enforcement agencies such as the Florida Police Chiefs Association, have come out against the measure. In Jacksonville Wednesday, Jennifer “Cookie” Pritt, executive director of the organization, said during a press conference, “Before you vote, ask yourself one question: Where will the money for your local police come from? If no one can give you a straight answer, that tells you what you need to know about Amendment 3.”
DeSantis insisted again that if Amendment 3 passes, he would work with the Legislature to create a fund for fiscally constrained and other “bedroom” communities in places like the Tampa Bay area where they could apply for grants if they need more revenue for “critical needs” — to hire more police officers, for example.
The Legislature killed a provision of the governor’s original proposal that would have created a state trust fund to help local governments cover revenue shortfalls. There is no guarantee lawmakers would agree to do that in the approximately two months DeSantis has left in office.
The governor expressed concern that the Republican turnout hasn’t “been as strong as we would like to see” in vote-by-mail and early voting numbers that have come in. More than 3.7 million Floridians have voted so far, according to the University of Florida Election Lab, with registered Republicans holding a 1.2% lead over registered Democrats, 40.2%-39% (independent and third party registered voters amount to 21% of the state’s vote total to date).
The Republican Party of Florida has endorsed Amendment 3, while the Florida Democratic Party has opposes the measure.
Campaign spending has been heavily titled towards the pro-Amendment 3 forces. A political committee formed by the Florida Realtors to support it has raised more than $21.5 million, according to state election records.  The two political committees opposing Amendment 3, Floridians for Shared Prosperity and Vote No on 3 Florida, have raised a combined $1.3 million.
“I think that we need to do a better job of early voting,” DeSantis said. “Republicans have some work to do, and you guys just got to get out there and vote and then let the people’s will carry the day.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Lack of major property tax relief in Kansas prompts fingerpointing in governor’s race
text:
Democrat Cindy Holscher and Republican Ty Masterson appear at the Sept. 12, 2026, debate at the Kansas State Fair. The two rivals for governor agree on the need to reduce property taxes for homeowners but clash on the details. (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Kansas Senate President Ty Masterson shared with television viewers Jan. 12, 2021, a vision for how Republicans could deal with runaway property taxes.
In the GOP reply to Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly’s State of the State speech, Masterson promised GOP lawmakers would address the burden of $5.4 billion in property taxes collected statewide at that time. It wasn’t an unimaginable political feat given Masterson’s authority over the GOP supermajority in the Senate and House Speaker Dan Hawkins’ control of the two-thirds Republican majority in the House.
It was a politically astute pledge, because polling consistently affirmed property tax applied to homeowners was the most hated, relative to sales and income taxes.
“We must work to enact meaningful property tax reform to allow seniors and families to stay in their homes,” Masterson vowed.
Senate President Ty Masterson, the 2026 Republican nominee for governor, promises in a 2021 video message to make property tax reform a top legislative priority. (Kansas Reflector screen capture of Kansas Legislature video)
The Legislature spent the next five years nibbling on the edge of reform, but annual statewide revenue from property taxes ballooned to $6.6 billion by 2025. Legislators continued to hear from folks outraged by double-digit escalation of property valuations that triggered tax increases even when mill levies remained flat.
Sen. Cindy Holscher, the Democratic Party’s nominee for governor, said Masterson and Hawkins failed to leverage their Republican supermajorities to grapple with property taxes in the manner they did to slash state income taxes and trim the state’s sales tax on groceries. In the 2026 legislative session, the House and Senate ran into gridlock as they took turns voting down competing GOP property tax bills.
“Ty Masterson has had years as Senate president, with a Republican supermajority behind him, and time and again he has repeatedly failed to deliver the property tax relief Kansans need,” Holscher said. “He said, ‘We can do whatever we want because we’re in charge.’ He either doesn’t want to do this or doesn’t know how.”
Masterson, the Republican gubernatorial nominee, joined the outcry. He said he was disappointed obstinate Democrats and “phony Republicans” stood in the way of efforts to limit the ability of school, city and county officials to pile up property tax revenue.
“The truth of why your taxes are so high … people like Cindy have not met one of your tax dollars she didn’t want to spend two of. You have to put constraints on the local government,” Masterson said. “I want to make your life more affordable and property taxes is a big part of that.”
In 1997, residential property owners in Kansas accounted for 38% of property tax revenue, while commercial property owners picked up 62%. The accumulation of tax exemptions for businesses reversed the math. By 2024, residential owners paid 57% of the property tax bill in Kansas and commercial property owners in the state covered 43%.
 
The track record
The Legislature during the past five years considered dozens of ideas for modifying the property tax landscape, but momentum for reform was tempered by the reality that local government received the majority of its funding from property tax. Cities and counties objected to the Legislature wading into their funding stream.
In 2021, the Legislature approved a “truth in taxation” law preventing cities, counties or townships from raising property tax revenue above the previous year’s inflation-adjusted total without mailing advance notice to taxpayers and conducting public hearings before voting on property tax changes.
State lawmakers in 2022 agreed to provide property tax reimbursements to retail business owners subjected to shutdown orders during the COVID-19 pandemic. Attempts by the Legislature to implement vehicle property tax relief prompted vetoes by Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly. Legislators did raise the residential exemption on property taxes to fund K-12 public schools from $20,000 to $40,000. That saved the average homeowner about $46 per year. Meanwhile, the Legislature approved property tax exemptions for telecommunications equipment.
In 2023, lawmakers debated, but failed to pass, an amendment to the Kansas Constitution to cap growth in property valuations that were the cause of higher tax bills for many homeowners.
In 2024, Kelly signed a measure raising the residential property tax exemption to $75,000 when calculating the 20-mill levy for aid to K-12 public schools. The Legislature’s focus that year was on cutting state income taxes. During a special session, the Legislature and governor agreed to a $1.2 billion, three-year reduction.
The Legislature voted in 2025 to eliminate 1.5 mills of state property tax levies relied on to finance state building construction projects. But that $80 million annual reduction in state property tax collections did nothing to change the reality that local governments continued to depend on property taxes for the vast majority of operating revenue. Kansas did adopt a property tax exemption in 2025 for off-road vehicles, boats and trailers.
In 2026, the House and Senate clashed for months without finding consensus on a sweeping property tax fix.
With Masterson’s blessing, the Senate tried to bulldoze through the legislative process an amendment to the Kansas Constitution limiting increases in annual assessment of property values to 3%. The House declined to endorse that approach. Instead, the House sought to prevent local units of government from increasing revenue from property taxes by more than 3% annually. Amid that debate, proposals calling for phasing out the property tax and replacing that revenue with a higher sales tax floundered.
Kelly vetoed a bill in the 2026 session that would have capped city and county spending increases at 3% or the rate of inflation and would have authorized Kansans to file signature petitions to block local property tax increases above that threshold. The governor dismissed the measure as evidence of the legislative leadership’s “false promise” of meaningful property tax reform.
Instead, she encouraged the Legislature to double to $150,000 the portion of a home’s value not subject to property taxes for schools. She recommended creation of a $60 million state fund to reward cities or counties that held budget increases to less than 3%.
 
Sen. Cindy Holscher says many of the Republicans’ ideas for property tax cuts amount to “gimmicks.” (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector)
Plans for change
Masterson, who has said during the governor’s race that property tax reform was a top priority, offered voters a “Homeowners Bill of Rights” that would guide the Republican if he were elected governor Nov. 3.
The blueprint would be anchored by a constitutional amendment to cap at 3% annual growth in the valuation of taxable property. In the alternative, the amendment would enable the Legislature to impose a limit on property tax rates. Constitutional amendments require consent from two-thirds of the House and Senate before placed on a statewide ballot.
“I have a neighbor. He’s spending more than double the property tax alone than he had been for his entire mortgage, interest, insurance taxes combined,” Masterson said. “At the same time, that’s putting such a load on our young people to afford housing, and homeownership is the underpinning of the middle class of any country. Our first-time average homeowner is now close to 40, and that’s just not acceptable.”
Masterson, who has represented Andover in the Legislature for 20 years, said he wanted local taxing jurisdictions to secure direct voter consent for “unreasonable” budget increases linked to property tax revenue. He would freeze or reduce property taxes for senior citizens and work toward inhibiting Kansans from being “taxed out” of a home, farm or business.
Holscher, an Overland Park resident elected to the Legislature in 2016, said much of the GOP’s strategy for property tax reform amount to “gimmicks” or concepts designed to financially starve local governments responsible for delivering essential public services.
“They squeeze the balloon, they shuffle the responsibility somewhere else, and it makes it harder for our local levels to raise the revenue they need for their critical services,” she said.
Holscher recommended the Legislature provide funding to fully meet its obligation to finance special education programs in K-12 public schools. When the state avoided its responsibility to students, she said, local school boards were forced to dip deeper into property tax revenue to cover program costs.
“Special education hasn’t been fully funded since 2011,” she said. “We’re federally mandated to fund it. When we don’t do that, that burden gets shifted to the local level.”
The Democratic senator said Kansas ought to lower the taxed percentage of home values from 11.5% to 9%, which would deliver property tax relief to homeowners across all income levels. In addition, Holscher recommended restraining the issuance of tax breaks to wealthy business owners. She also support specific property tax exemptions for seniors and disabled veterans.
